Q: How can I efficiently check if an element exists more than once in an array? A:

Your current code will not work if you will have even number of repetitions (as @wjandrea suggested in comment)

I would use two sets for this

  • one for "seen before"
  • other for duplicated.

In loop check if i in seen_before: duplicated.add(i) and later seen_before.add(i)

If you need unique then use set(nums) ^ duplicated.
Or set(nums) - duplicated as noticed @khelwood.

Example code with more numbers 3

nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1, 3]

seen_before = set()
duplicated = set()

for i in nums:
    if i in seen_before:
        duplicated.add(i)
    # else:
    seen_before.add(i)

#unique = set(nums) ^ duplicated
unique = set(nums) - duplicated  # as noticed @khelwood

print(f"{nums = }")
print(f"{duplicated = }")
print(f"{unique = }")

Result:

nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1, 3]
duplicated = {2, 3}
unique = {1, 4, 7, 8}

Q: Technical insights on migrating from Vue 3 to React: Benefits in predictability and maintenance A:

React has bigger ecosystem but no architectural or technical advantages over Vue that could justify the migration. Both are perfectly suitable for developing a large application.

As long as you don't heavily rely on a library that is exclusive to React (e.g. React Native, Next.js or some UI lib), there is no point in this sort of migration, unless those responsible for the decision have a personal interest in it - financial, professional, ideological, or otherwise.

Existing answers already have good points, I'll just focus on the important parts.

1.

This totally depends on code quality and conventions in a project. Vue doesn't oppose unidirectional flow by design, these rules aren't supposed to be broken, this includes deep object mutations.

Pinia guidelines favour direct mutation of a state, despite this leads to the same problem as prop mutations and previously was explicitly discouraged in Vuex, which had been succeeded by Pinia. Since Pinia actions fully replaced both Vuex actions and mutations, a safe declarative convention is to limit all state mutations to actions. This way any mutation can be narrowed down to a dispatched action and debugged via a breakpoint.

Also the mutations are debuggable. Even if this can't be handled with Vue devtools alone, a simple breakpoint in a watcher can give a call stack and help tracking a mutation. If it's not enough, there are specific debugging options.

2.

Choosing watch over watchEffect and shallow over deep reactivity API is enough for it to not be magical. On the other side, useEffect and other hooks contribute to cognitive load and can result in messy, error-prone dependency graph.

3.

No specific problems here besides the conventions that can be enforced through a linter and code style guidelines. Vue composables are subject to similar lifecycle restrictions and should be used in component setup, unless proven otherwise.

That Vue allows for the use of reactivity API outside a component for global state (and therefore reactivity-based composables) is a major benefit of the framework that React doesn't have a built-in counterpart for, certainly not a downside.

4.

This had been a long-term problem that could be expected from a DSL (which Vue template language is) that is currently considered resolved, as the use of vue-tsc has become the de facto standard. Either way, JSX/TSX is nearly a first-grade citizen in Vue. HOCs aren't idiomatic in Vue but can be used with JSX/TSX if necessary.

As for Pinia as the new standard in Vue, it's especially missed in a React project for me. Zustand and Valtio (let alone Redux) are less than optimal replacements in terms of DX.

TL;DR: I'd be extremely cautious about anyone who suggests migrating between the frameworks of the big three for a project with up-to-date codebase. I'd assume they are either pursuing their own goals, not competent enough for the job, or all of the above.

Q: SeleniumBase - Unable to select a value from a dropdown using value, text,index A:

According to the docs, you should be using

self.switch_to_frame("iframe")

to switch to an IFRAME.

So your code should look like

class MyTestClass(BaseCase):
    def test_demo_site(self):
      self.get(...)
      self.switch_to_frame("#icims_content_iframe") # this line was updated
      self.type("//*[@id='PersonProfileFields.FirstName']", "Saul")
      self.click("//a[@id='-1_PersonProfileFields.AddressCountry_icimsDropdown']")
      self.type("[aria-controls='-1_PersonProfileFields.AddressCountry_dropdown-results']", "India")
      self.click("li[title='India']")
      ...

When you are done working in that IFRAME, make sure you call self.switch_to_default_content() to come back out of the IFRAME context.

Q: Unable to activate MSFT Fabric Trial Capacity A:

I had this same issue yesterday and lots of these threads exist without the solution. Here's the solution: You have to go into licensing in the M365 admin portal and add "Fabric Free" licenses and allocate them to your users. In my case, we have an F64 capacity and MS told us users could access reports for this without a PBI license, which is true. However, they must have a Fabric Free license to view the content. These are free but you still have to go through the process - in our case we used a corporate credit card for 200 licenses of Fabric Free, which didn't actually charge the card. Once this was done and the license allocated, the users could access the published content from the F64 capacity. Hope this helps others.

Q: How to set window size in Selenium Base in CDP Mode? A:

Use sb.cdp.set_window_rect(x, y, width, height). (All 4 parameters need to be set.) Eg:

from seleniumbase import SB

with SB(uc=True, test=True) as sb:
    url = "https://bot-detector.rebrowser.net/"
    sb.activate_cdp_mode(url)
    sb.cdp.set_window_rect(10, 10, 1200, 700)
    sb.sleep(10)
